b: Writing documentation Every page of the documentation site is a Markdown file under docs/. The generator src/tools/docsite turns them into the static site under site/docs/. There is no framework and nothing is fetched at runtime; the pages render in Wren itself. The workflow Write or edit a .md file under docs/. If the page is new, add it to docs/_nav.txt so it appears in the sidebar where you want it. A page you forget is still generated and linked (it lands in a "More" section), so nothing is lost, but the order and the section are up to you. Run tools\docs_site.ps1. It regenerates site/docs/ and checks that every internal link and anchor resolves. Commit the .md and the regenerated site/docs/. The generation is deterministic (same input, same bytes), and CI fails if site/docs/ is out of date — the same rule as tools\changelog.ps1 -Check. The sidebar: docs/_nav.txt The file lists the sections and the pages in each, in the order they appear. Its own header documents the format. In short: Section Title page.md a page whose label is its first heading page.md Label a page with an explicit sidebar label dir/* Label every .md of a directory, as a sub-group (an _index.md or README.md leads it) The Markdown it understands The generator implements the slice of CommonMark and GitHub-flavored Markdown the docs use: Headings # to ######. Accessibility Wren is read by screen readers (NVDA, Narrator, JAWS) and other assistive technologies through UI Automation. The toolkit makes the accessibility tree of the interface from its boxes and hands it to AccessKit (ext/gui_toolkit/docs/accessibility.md); Wren says what only a browser knows. Build The assembly crate native/wren_native builds the toolkit's adapter (ext/gui_toolkit/native/a11y, AccessKit 0.25 and its Windows adapter) into wren_native.lib (feature a11y: a program links one Rust static library; see docs/architecture.md, "The Rust library"), and build.bat builds with -define:A11Y_ACCESSKIT=true -define:A11Y_NATIVE_LINK=false. The crates are listed in native/rust-crates.txt (about:licenses). Nothing is built until an assistive technology asks for a window's tree; from then on each frame sends the nodes that changed. wren ctl stats --json says what was sent: a11yUpdates, a11yRefused, a11yLastNodes, a11yNodes. Module async Promises, microtasks, buffers and host objects: the asynchronous core every other module builds on. A promise's value is an i64 (a number, or the handle of a buffer or another object) plus a string (an error message, a text result). Reactions run as microtasks once it settles. There are no closures in Wasm, so then does not create a chained promise: a reaction that passes a result on resolves a promise of its own. A buffer is the ArrayBuffer of this platform: bytes owned by the browser, passed between APIs without copies into the module's memory (fetch bodies, messages, socket frames), counted against page.max_fetch_bytes. Module canvas Canvas 2D (HTML §4.12.5): the 2D rendering context of canvas and OffscreenCanvas, drawn by a software rasterizer (package canvas2d) into a premultiplied RGBA8 bitmap that the shell shows as a texture, updated only when the drawing changed. Module credentials Web Authentication Level 3 (passkeys, security keys) and the Credential Management container it hangs off (navigator.credentials). The options are passed in their standard JSON form (PublicKeyCredentialCreationOptionsJSON / PublicKeyCredentialRequestOptionsJSON: binary members in base64url), which is what a server sends: a module can hand it over as is. The browser checks them, decides the RP ID (a registrable domain suffix of the document's domain), builds clientDataJSON, and asks the operating system's authenticators (Windows: Windows Hello, security keys, a phone), whose dialog the user answers. Only a secure context may call these (SecurityError otherwise); a ceremony needs a recent key press or click in the page (security.webauthn.require_user_activation) and the page's tab shown in the focused window (security.webauthn.require_focus), else NotAllowedError; one ceremony at a time per document. Rejections use the Error codes: Not_Allowed (cancelled, timed out, no credential, refused), Invalid_State (an excluded credential exists), Not_Supported, Security (RP ID), Type (malformed options), Abort (the signal's reason), Encoding (invalid base64url). Exposed to: Window. Source: api/credentials.widl. Types handle PublicKeyCredential : Object A PublicKeyCredential: the authenticator's answer, with its response (attestation or assertion). Architecture How Wren is put together, and the rules that keep it from breaking as it grows. For the overview, the build and the feature list, see the README. The rules that keep it from breaking at scale One ownership tree. process → tab → navigation → page → (instances, DOM, requests, timers). Everything a page starts is registered in its scope (src/base/scope.odin); closing a tab or navigating is scope_close. Cleanups run newest first, children before parents, so nothing outlives what it points to. Scopes are main-thread only. Handles, never pointers, cross boundaries. Handle = generation << 32 | index, 0 is invalid. A destroyed or recycled slot fails to resolve. Late network events, timers and listener callbacks for dead objects are dropped, not delivered to reused memory. Pool objects never move (chunked), so ^T stays valid until removed. Single UI thread, everything else posts. The network stack's threads, the image decoders, the layout and style threads and the blocking pool only push events and host.post back to the loop; every user-visible callback runs on the loop thread. The DOM and the Wasm instances of a page live on the UI thread (workers have their own store). b: Driving Wren with CDP and WebDriver BiDi Wren can be driven by the standard automation tools — Puppeteer, Playwright (connectOverCDP or the BiDi transport), Chrome DevTools, and WebDriver BiDi clients — over a local WebSocket. An adapter translates their messages onto the same command engine wren ctl uses (docs/remote.md): there is one control path, not two. Turning it on The adapter is off by default. Turn it on for one run with a command-line flag, or always with a preference: wren --remote-debugging-port=9222 --headless about:blank wren --remote-debugging-port=9222 https://example.com/ --remote-debugging-port=N listens on port N. --remote-debugging-port with no number (or port 0) lets the system pick a free one; it is written to DevToolsActivePort in the profile, as Chrome does (a tool reads it there). --remote-debugging-address=ADDR is accepted but only loopback is honoured: the server always binds 127.0.0.1. A remote bind is a security hazard this build does not offer; a non-loopback address is a warning, not an error. The preference remote.cdp.enabled turns it on at every start (port remote.cdp.port, 0 = the system picks one). remote.cdp.max_clients (8) is how many tools may connect at once. --headless and --remote-debugging-port go together naturally (a driven Wren needs no window), but either works alone. b: bigint: arbitrary-precision integers for the JavaScript engine src/engine/bigint is the ECMAScript BigInt arithmetic, written natively in Odin. The JavaScript engine used to get this from QuickJS's C running inside WebAssembly; this package replaces it with a native implementation that gives identical numeric results and reads like Odin instead of transcribed C. It is allocation-aware: every operation allocates its result through context.allocator, so the engine injects the realm's allocator and frees results with destroy. No OS dependency — it builds for windows_amd64, linux_amd64 and freestanding_wasm32. Representation Sign-magnitude, little-endian u32 limbs, always normalized (no leading zero limb; zero is the empty magnitude with neg = false). This is the natural Odin shape and keeps the arithmetic obvious. The one place the choice shows is the bitwise operators: ECMAScript defines & | ^ ~ and >> as if a BigInt were an infinite two's-complement integer, so those operations convert each operand to its two's-complement limb view over a common width, apply the op, and convert back (bits.odin). import bi "wb:engine/bigint" a := bi.from_i64(1_000_000_007) b, _ := bi.from_string("340282366920938463463374607431768211456", 10) // 2^128 defer bi.destroy(&a) defer bi.destroy(&b) p := bi.mul(a, b); defer bi.destroy(&p) q := bi.div(p, a); defer bi.destroy(&q) // == b s :=

t: datetime (package jsdate): the JavaScript engine's Date
b: datetime (package jsdate): the JavaScript engine's Date src/engine/datetime is the ECMAScript Date calendar and string handling, written natively in Odin (the package is named jsdate so it never collides with core:time/datetime). It is ported from QuickJS-ng and produces the same results as QuickJS over the whole valid range, so Date behaves identically without the C that used to run in WebAssembly. Time values are milliseconds since the Unix epoch as f64, NaN for an invalid Date; the valid range is ±8.64 × 10¹⁵ ms (about ±273 790 years). Fields use the ECMAScript order [year, month(0–11), day(1–31), hour, min, sec, ms, weekday, tz-minutes]. The package is allocation-free and has no OS dependency, so it builds for windows_amd64, linux_amd64 and freestanding_wasm32. The one thing it cannot compute on its own — the local time zone offset — is a host callback. The time zone callback import jsdate "wb:engine/datetime" jsdate.timezone_offset_proc = proc "contextless" (time_ms: i64) -> int { return host_get_timezone_offset(time_ms) // minutes west of UTC, i.e. getTimezoneOffset(t) } This is the exact role of js.timezone_offset in the Wren host. When the callback is nil, local time equals UTC, so UTC-only code (and tests) work with no host wired up. Moteur JavaScript — front-end E1 (src/engine/frontend) Le paquet frontend est la moitié « amont » du moteur JavaScript écrit en Odin. Il transforme du source ECMAScript en bytecode QuickJS-ng 0.17, identique octet pour octet à ce que produit JS_WriteObject (BC_VERSION 28, drapeaux JS_WRITE_OBJ_BYTECODE | JS_WRITE_OBJ_STRIP_SOURCE). L'autre moitié (E2 : valeurs, objets, GC, interpréteur, fonctions natives) relit ce bytecode. Les deux moitiés ne se rencontrent qu'au format de bytecode : opcodes.odin, atoms.odin, serialize.odin. Le paquet compile pour windows_amd64, linux_amd64 et freestanding_wasm32. Toute allocation passe par l'allocateur injecté (une arène libère une compilation entière d'un coup). Aucun appel OS, aucune libc. Il réutilise les paquets feuilles numconv (littéraux numériques) et unicode (ucd, données Unicode 17.0.0). Pourquoi un portage direct du compilateur QuickJS La première version passait par un AST (lexer, parseur, résolveur, émetteur séparés ; voir l'historique git, commit dc13ba87). Elle ne pouvait pas atteindre la parité octet : QuickJS émet en une seule passe pendant le parse, et son bytecode dépend de cet ordre exact. Exemples : les réécritures du dernier opcode émis (get_lvalue, optional chaining, delete), l'ordre de création des variables et des portées, les OP_scope_get_var posés avant que la portée ne soit connue,

t: numconv: float64 ↔ string for the JavaScript engine
b: numconv: float64 ↔ string for the JavaScript engine src/engine/numconv is the part of the JavaScript engine that turns a float64 into the string a script sees (String(x), Number.prototype.toString/toFixed/toExponential/toPrecision) and parses a string back into a float64 (Number(s), parseFloat, parseInt). It is written natively in Odin, ported deliberately from QuickJS-ng's dtoa.c (Fabrice Bellard, MIT), and produces the same bytes as QuickJS for every finite f64 and every radix 2–36, so the engine's number output never depends on the C that used to run inside WebAssembly. It is allocation-free: the string producers write into a caller buffer and return the length, the parsers read a string, and the bignum scratch that the algorithm needs lives on fixed stack arrays (what QuickJS kept in JSDTOATempMem/JSATODTempMem). That is what lets the package build for windows_amd64, linux_amd64 and freestanding_wasm32 with no allocator and no OS. Using it import nc "wb:engine/numconv" buf: [nc.MAX_STR_LEN]u8 // always big enough for any dtoa output n := nc.f64_to_shortest(buf[:], 3.14) // "3.14" (String(x), base 10) n = nc.f64_to_radix(buf[:], 255, 16) // "ff" (Number.prototype.toString(16)) n = nc.f64_to_fixed(buf[:], 1.5, 3) // "1.500" (toFixed(3)) n = nc.f64_to_exponential(buf[:], 12345, 2) // "1.23e+4" (toExponential(2)) n = nc.f64_to_precision(buf[:], 12345, 3) // "1.23e+4"

engine/regexp Odin port of QuickJS-ng's libregexp: a full ECMAScript regular-expression parser and bytecode compiler, plus a bounded backtracking interpreter. It replaces the C engine and leans on the language — tagged opcodes, interval character sets, caller-supplied allocators, an explicit (non-recursive) backtrack stack — so it builds for windows_amd64, linux_amd64 and freestanding_wasm32 with no libc. import rx "wb:engine/regexp" API re, err := rx.compile(pattern, flags, allocator) // flags: rx.Flags bit_set defer rx.destroy(&re) if err.message != "" { /* compile error at err.pos */ } caps: rx.Captures st := rx.exec_search(&re, rx.input_utf16(units), start, &caps, limits, allocator) // st is .Match / .No_Match / .Out_Of_Steps / .Stack_Overflow if st == .Match { whole := caps.groups[0] // {start, end} in code-unit offsets, or {-1,-1} if unset idx, ok := rx.named_group_index(&re, "year") } Flags d g i m s u v y — rx.parse_flags("gims") → rx.Flags; rx.flags_to_string. Input is a slice of code units, either UTF-16 (rx.input_utf16, JS semantics, offsets are UTF-16 indices) or UTF-8 (rx.input_utf8 / rx.input_utf8_string, offsets are byte indices). Surrogate pairs combine only in unicode mode. exec tries exactly one start offset; exec_search scans forward from start (and respects the sticky y flag, which forbids advancing). Captures are reported in code-unit offsets;

engine/unicode (ucd) Odin port of QuickJS-ng's libunicode. It provides the Unicode data the regexp engine and the JS lexer need: character-set intervals, case conversion / folding / the ECMAScript regexp canonicalize, the identifier and whitespace predicates, the \p{} property / general-category / script sets, and the four normalization forms. The package is named ucd (not unicode) so it does not collide with core:unicode. Import it with an alias: import ucd "wb:engine/unicode" It compiles for windows_amd64, linux_amd64 and freestanding_wasm32. Nothing in the runtime path touches the OS; every allocation goes through a caller-supplied allocator (pass an arena to free a whole build at once). The only hosted-only file is settings.odin (the preference registry needs an OS); it is excluded from the freestanding build with a #+build tag. Data: generated, pinned, never copied The tables are generated from the authoritative Unicode Character Database, not copied from QuickJS's libunicode-table.h: tools/gen_unicode.ps1 downloads the pinned UCD files for a fixed Unicode release (17.0.0, the version QuickJS-ng 0.17 ships), verifies each file's SHA-256 (the same idiom as tools/build_js.ps1), then runs the generator. src/engine/unicode/gen/ (an Odin program) parses the UCD text and writes tables_generated.odin: sorted half-open interval runs for every property / category / script, simple

t: Translating Wren: how the texts are written
b: Translating Wren: how the texts are written Every text the user reads goes through the i18n package (src/i18n), so that a language can be added without going through the code again. Today English is the only language and tr returns its argument: writing the texts the right way now is what makes the translation cheap later. The plan and the open questions are in the maintainer's notes ("Internationalisation"). import "wb:i18n" label := i18n.tr("Open in a new tab") close := i18n.tr("tab strip", "Close") // a context for the translator, never shown text := fmt.tprintf(i18n.tr(count, "%d request", "%d requests"), count) // singular, plural, by count One name, tr, a procedure group: the compiler picks the form from the arguments (a text; a context and a text; a count and two forms). The English text is the key: no identifier to invent, and the code reads as before. English only, and no cost English is the only language for now, and the package has no code to load another one yet. tr returns its argument, a string literal in the executable's read-only data: no lookup, no allocation, no copy, and the texts stay side by side where the linker put them. A test (english_returns_the_same_bytes) keeps it that way. A language, when there is one, must not cost more than that, because the interface is drawn every frame and tr runs for every label: One blob, not many strings. The translations

Wren documentation Wren is a web browser written from scratch in Odin, for Windows, where WebAssembly is the only execution engine — JavaScript included. The scripts of a page run in QuickJS-ng compiled to WebAssembly, inside the same Wasmtime sandbox, memory cap and interruption as every other module. The web platform itself (DOM, CSS, layout, painting, Fetch, the shell) is native Odin, drawn on Direct3D 11. There is no Chromium underneath. A page can also be a single .wasm file that calls the browser directly, through imports generated from Web IDL: see Web API. Installing Wren is a single executable for Windows x64. There is no installer to run as administrator: Download the latest .zip from the releases page and unzip it anywhere, then run wren.exe. Or install it from winget: winget install Froment.Wren. Every version is free during the beta. A supporter licence unlocks nothing; it keeps the work going. Driving Wren You rarely need to click to test a page. Wren ships one executable that is also its own client: wren ctl run --size 1280x800 --shot out.png https://example.com/ # one page, one capture wren ctl start --size 1280x800 # a session you keep driving wren ctl nav https://example.com/ wren ctl shot page.png wren ctl stop The same browser can be driven by Puppeteer and Playwright over the Chrome DevTools Protocol: wren --remote-debugging-port=9222 --headless

b: Writing Wren's JavaScript glue in Odin Wren's JavaScript engine is QuickJS-ng compiled to one WebAssembly module (build/js/wren_js.wasm), run by Wasmtime. Around the engine sits the glue: the code that implements the web platform's objects as QuickJS native functions and wires them to the browser's wr_* imports. Wren 0.3.0 Wren 0.3.0 compiles JavaScript to WebAssembly, loads iframes and no longer lets a busy page freeze the browser. WebAssembly is still the only execution engine: hot JavaScript functions are compiled to Wasm modules while the page runs, in the same sandbox. This is still a beta, under development, and Windows-only. Highlights A JIT for JavaScript that produces WebAssembly. Hot functions and loops of QuickJS-ng are compiled to Wasm modules on background threads, then by Wasmtime (Cranelift); guards fall back to the interpreter exactly. Modules are position-independent, shared by every page and kept in the disk cache: a second tab or a reload compiles nothing. Octane about 1.75 times as fast as the interpreter (navier-stokes ×4, zlib ×2.7), loops and property accesses ×4 to ×6, DOM getters twice as fast. test262 and web-platform-tests show no regression, with everything compiled at once too. Iframes. Each <iframe> is a document of its own, with its origin, its scripts and its JavaScript engine instance: src, srcdoc, sandbox, allow (Permissions Policy), postMessage, cross-origin WindowProxy limits, X-Frame-Options and frame-ancestors, forms and links aimed at a named frame, storage and HTTP cache partitioned by top-level site. b: SharedArrayBuffer between realms: the trial of tranche 4 Question: can a page and its workers share a SharedArrayBuffer? That means postMessage sends the same bytes, not a copy, and Atomics.wait / Atomics.notify work between them. Wren would expose it under COOP/COEP (crossOriginIsolated). What was tried The test is src/wasm/shared_memory_test.odin (two_stores_share_a_memory_and_wait_for_each_other). The setup is the one a page and a worker would have: two Wasm instances, each in its own Wasmtime store and on its own thread. Wasmtime 49 has the threads proposal and shared memories turned on. Both instances import one wasmtime_sharedmemory. One thread blocks in memory.atomic.wait32, the instruction behind Atomics.wait. The other thread does i32.atomic.store, then memory.atomic.notify. Publishing Wren on winget Wren can be offered through the Windows Package Manager (winget), so that winget install FromentSoftware.Wren installs it. This is not automatic: a published release does not reach winget on its own. The step below makes the manifest; the submission to Microsoft's winget-pkgs repository is a manual pull request, and only Sacha does it. There is no Microsoft Store package (the Store needs an MSIX and a developer account; the release is a single portable .exe, which winget supports directly as a portable installer). What the release is Every release publishes one file, wren-<version>-windows-x64.exe (see tools\package.ps1 and .github\workflows\release.yml), plus SHA256SUMS.txt with its SHA-256. It is not an installer: it is the program itself, which carries its licences, its version and the Visual C++ runtime it needs, and integrates into the desktop from within (Setup).
